bib.title: The Art of Building Verifiers for Computer Use Agents

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: All 33 pages (89,610 chars) extracted and read, main text and appendices A to C. The late appendix tables (rubric examples, error taxonomy, Tables 15-18) I only skimmed.

SOURCE: "The Art of Building Verifiers for Computer Use Agents". First author Corby Rosset (Microsoft Research); co-authors Pratyusha Sharma, Andrew Zhao, Ahmed Awadallah (Microsoft Research) and Miguel Gonzalez-Fernandez (Browserbase). arXiv 2604.06240v1, 5 Apr 2026. Venue is "Preprint. Under review." The triage name "Universal Verifier" is the paper's name for its system, not its title.

CORE CLAIM: A trajectory verifier for computer-use agents reaches human-level agreement through four design choices. (1) Rubrics with specific, non-overlapping criteria, generated from the task alone, separately from scoring. (2) Separate process (rubric score) and outcome (binary) rewards. (3) Controllable versus uncontrollable failures, scored without cascading errors. (4) Per-criterion top-k screenshot selection so all screenshots are attended to. The authors say the gain is architectural, not from a stronger model.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. Outcome Cohen's κ against human labels, Universal Verifier (UV, GPT-5.2): 0.64 on the internal set (140 Fara-7B trajectories from WebTailBench, in-house experts) and 0.58 on the Browserbase Online-Mind2Web (OM2W) set (106 Fara-7B trajectories, 2 annotators each). WebJudge (o4-mini) scores 0.44 and 0.26. WebVoyager (GPT-4o) scores 0.31 and 0.13. (Table 2, p8)
2. Outcome false positive rate (FPR), same setup. UV: 0.01 internal, 0.08 Browserbase. WebVoyager (GPT-4o): 0.45 and 0.60. WebJudge (o4-mini): 0.22 and 0.40. (Table 2)
3. Backbone swap. Upgrading WebVoyager and WebJudge to GPT-5.2 cuts WebVoyager outcome FPR from 0.45 to 0.10 (internal). FNR rises from 0.24 to 0.44, and κ goes only from 0.31 to 0.43, still below 0.64. WebJudge FNR rises from 0.33 to 0.57. (Table 2, p8; B.3, p22)
4. Humans versus UV on Browserbase. UV outcome κ of 0.58 and process κ of 0.43 fall within the inter-annotator ranges of 0.53–0.57 and 0.36–0.45. Process agreement is lower than outcome throughout (internal process κ 0.59, Browserbase 0.43).
5. Auto-research (Claude Code v2.1.87, Opus 4.6, internal set). Starting from blank prompts it plateaus at κ≈0.55, "70% of expert quality in 5% of the time". The human expert took 32 experiments over three weeks to reach κ≈0.7. Started from the expert's best verifier, it surpassed the expert peak under a no-FPR-increase rule. Outcome κ ranged 0.64–0.71 across identical prompts, so run-to-run noise is large (p25).
Also: when annotators saw the UV's reasoning, outcome κ rose from 0.39 to 0.63. 16.6% of annotator outcome judgements flipped (34 flips, 31 of them success to failure). (p8, B.2)

QUOTES
- "We conclude UV's advantage stems from its screenshot scoring design, not merely from using a stronger model" (p8)
- "Generating the rubric and scoring it in a single LLM call leads the model to create criteria tailored to the agent's behavior." (p4)

LIMITS
- The UV is a prompted GPT-5.2 pipeline of about 3,000 lines of code and 2,000 lines of prompts, designed by one expert (the first author). The ablation sets are small (n=140 and n=106).
- Human labels come from in-house experts and one vendor. The authors concede that outcome "success" is subjective, and they define it as primary intent.
- The headline "near zero" FPR comes with FNR of 0.32 internal and 0.31 Browserbase, so the UV is conservative. The Browserbase outcome FPR is 0.08, not near zero.
- At scale (Table 3), the UV is the reference label, not human truth. Against the UV, native verifiers have FPR above 20%.
- The "70% of expert" auto-research result is a single setup. The paper notes that parts of the work were AI-generated.
- On AgentRewardBench, the check is 8 of 30 human-labelled successes judged false positives by the authors' own guidelines (≈0.27).
- It does not compare against trained verifiers or other domains such as non-web or non-visual agents. Code and data are "will be available" at github.com/microsoft/fara.

BUILDS ON
- WebVoyager (He et al., ACL 2024) and WebJudge (Xue et al., 2025, "An illusion of progress?").
- AgentRewardBench (Lù et al., 2025) and AgentRx (Barke et al., 2026).
- Process versus outcome supervision: Uesato et al. 2022; Lightman et al. 2023 ("Let's verify step by step"); Stuhlmüller & Byun 2022 (Ought).
- Pan et al. 2024 (autonomous evaluation of digital agents).
- Auto-research: Karpathy 2026 autoresearch; Lu et al., Nature 2026.
- Agreement metric: Artstein & Poesio 2008.

BEST-FIT NOTE SECTION
The 06 headings are "Outcome and trajectory", "Grade the outcome by state, not by words", "Scoring tool calls", "Efficiency metrics", "Environment hygiene" and others. I did not read the note bodies. The best fit is "Outcome and trajectory" (process versus outcome rewards, uncontrollable environment failures). A second fit is "Environment hygiene" (blocked-by-environment cases). An eval note may fit the numbers better: 05-llm-as-judge or 15-calibration-against-human-labels (κ, FPR/FNR against humans, UV-blind versus UV-informed annotation, single-call rubric generate-and-score bias). 14-calibrating-judges-with-checks-and-critiques also fits for generating the rubric without seeing the trajectory and for two-pass scoring.

FIGURE CANDIDATE
Figure 1 (p1): outcome κ over experiments for the human expert and the two auto-research runs, with the structural jumps tagged. It shows both the iterate-against-human-labels loop and the auto-research gap. Alternative: Table 2 (p8) for the baseline comparison.

PROBLEMS: None with the extraction. No embedded instructions. Figure text is garbled but the captions are readable.
